short: CDC5L is the human orthologue of fission yeast Cdc5, a protein with two N-terminal Myb/SANT-like repeats whose main established job is not transcription at all: it is an essential component of the spliceosomal Prp19/CDC5L complex required for the second catalytic step of pre-mRNA splicing, and it is visible in cryo-EM structures of the human spliceosome. A site-specific DNA-binding activity was reported for the N-terminal region, and CDC5L also promotes G2/M progression and participates in the ATR-dependent S-phase checkpoint. Its motif evidence is weak: the two models in these databases disagree completely with each other, and one is inherited from an Arabidopsis protein rather than measured on human CDC5L. Treat any hit with caution.
long:
## The factors

CDC5L (also CDC5, CEF1) was named for Schizosaccharomyces pombe cdc5+, cloned in 1994 as an essential gene
whose product has homology to c-MYB [PMID:8313892]. The protein carries two Myb/SANT-like repeats near the N terminus -
fewer than the three repeats of c-MYB itself - followed by a long low-complexity C-terminal region with a
latent transcriptional activation domain [PMID:11082045]. A mammalian homologue was shown to regulate G2 progression and
mitotic entry [PMID:9468527]. There is a single human gene and no close paralogue, so within this family there is no
member ambiguity; the ambiguity is about whether the protein functions as a DNA-binding transcription
factor at all.

The best-established function is in splicing. CDC5L is the scaffold of a multiprotein complex in nuclear
extract - the CDC5L/Prp19 complex, containing PRPF19, PLRG1, BCAS2, CTNNBL1, HSPA8 and others - that joins
the spliceosome in an ATP-dependent step and is required for the second catalytic step of pre-mRNA
splicing [PMID:11101529]. Immunodepleting it blocks splicing product formation without preventing spliceosome assembly [PMID:11101529].
The complex is resolved in cryo-EM structures of the human catalytic spliceosome [PMID:29301961]. CDC5L also interacts
with ATR and is required for the S-phase cell-cycle checkpoint [PMID:19633697]. Orthologues behave similarly: Arabidopsis
CDC5 (AtCDC5) is part of the MOS4-associated complex (MAC) with MOS4 and PRL1, which is required for plant
innate immunity and for splicing and microRNA biogenesis [PMID:17575050,28947490]; AtCDC5 was shown to have DNA-binding activity [PMID:8917598,17575050],
which is where the plant-derived motif in these databases comes from [PMID:25215497]. CDC5L is broadly and constitutively
expressed, as befits a core splicing factor.

## The motif

There is no reliable consensus for human CDC5L, and this entry does not assert one. A 12-bp sequence bound
specifically and with high affinity by the N-terminal region of human Cdc5 was identified in 2000, together
with human genomic fragments containing similar sequences that bound with comparable specificity, and the
interaction could activate transcription in a reporter [PMID:11082045]. That paper explicitly noted that previous attempts
by others had failed to find a preferential binding site for Cdc5-family proteins [PMID:11082045], which sets the
expectation for how well-determined this specificity is.

The two models in this atlas disagree with one another, and the disagreement is the single most important
fact about this family. The CIS-BP model, M02698, has consensus GCGCTGAGC - and it is not measured on the
human protein: it is transferred from Arabidopsis thaliana CDC5 at 87% DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497]. The
Vierstra archetype AC0311:CDC5L:Myb/SANT has consensus GATTTAACATA [PMID:32728250], an AT-rich sequence with no resemblance
to the CIS-BP model. Family cohesion is 0.21, essentially no agreement, and neither model's best match in
any other family exceeds about 0.72. There are no JASPAR or HOCOMOCO models. So the honest description is
that this family contains two mutually inconsistent models, one of which is a cross-species inference and
the other of which is a footprint-derived archetype named for a factor whose footprints may reflect
something else entirely.

## Where it acts

There is no well-mapped genomic distribution for human CDC5L binding sites. The 2000 study recovered human
genomic fragments containing sequences related to its 12-bp site and suggested these are specific,
low-abundance sequences rather than a common promoter element [PMID:11082045], but genome-wide occupancy data for CDC5L as
a DNA-binding factor are essentially absent. Because CDC5L is abundant, nuclear and associated with
co-transcriptional splicing machinery, it is highly likely to crosslink to actively transcribed gene
bodies and promoters in ChIP experiments without binding DNA sequence-specifically. That is precisely the
situation in which a footprint- or ChIP-derived "CDC5L motif" is likely to be the motif of whatever else
occupies those regions. In Arabidopsis, AtCDC5 acts through the MAC complex on defence gene expression and
on splicing [PMID:17575050,28947490], again a mixture of direct and indirect routes.

## Biology and disease

Loss of Cdc5 function is lethal in fission yeast [PMID:8313892]. In mammalian cells, overexpressing CDC5L shortened G2,
and a dominant-negative mutant lacking the C-terminal activation domain slowed G2 progression and delayed
entry into mitosis [PMID:9468527]. The S-phase checkpoint function requires the CDC5L-ATR
interaction [PMID:19633697], linking it to the DNA damage response. In the Arabidopsis system, MAC components including
AtCDC5 are required for SNC1-mediated innate immunity [PMID:17575050] and for correct splicing under stress [PMID:28947490]. In human
disease, CDC5L is reported as overexpressed in several cancers, but the mechanistic accounts are
inconsistent and mostly correlative, and it is not established whether any such effect runs through DNA
binding rather than through splicing. There is no monogenic human disease attributed to CDC5L. The
literature is thin on the transcription-factor side and rich on the splicing side, and motif databases
reflect the former more confidently than the evidence supports.

## Reading a hit

Do not read a CDC5L hit as evidence that CDC5L binds your sequence. The two available models are mutually
contradictory (cohesion 0.21), which alone should prevent a specific call. The CIS-BP model is inherited
from Arabidopsis CDC5 at 87% DNA-binding-domain identity, so it reports a plant protein's preference, and
a GCGCTGAGC match in human sequence is at least as likely to be a coincidence or another Myb/SANT-type or
CRE-adjacent element. The Vierstra archetype is a footprint cluster labelled CDC5L; footprint archetypes
are named after the factor group that dominated a cluster, not after a demonstrated binder, and CDC5L's
abundance at transcribed regions makes an indirect explanation plausible. There is no paralogue problem,
but there is a class problem: CDC5L's demonstrated essential activity is in splicing, and a DNA match
gives you no purchase on that. If a CDC5L hit matters to your analysis, verify it directly rather than
relying on the database label.
caveats: The two models in this family contradict each other: CIS-BP gives GCGCTGAGC and the Vierstra archetype gives GATTTAACATA, with cohesion of only 0.21 and no JASPAR or HOCOMOCO model to arbitrate. The CIS-BP entry is not measured on human CDC5L at all - it is transferred from Arabidopsis thaliana CDC5 at 87% DNA-binding-domain identity - and the Vierstra entry is a footprint cluster named for CDC5L rather than a demonstrated binding preference. A 12-bp human Cdc5 site was reported once, but earlier attempts to find any preferential site for Cdc5-family proteins failed. CDC5L's established essential role is in pre-mRNA splicing, and as an abundant nuclear protein at transcribed regions it is a good candidate for indirect crosslinking. Treat any hit as unverified.

timeline.finding: Fission-yeast cdc5+ is cloned as an essential G2 gene whose product has a Myb-related N-terminal region; a fragment of it binds DNA-cellulose at low salt.
timeline.methods: Yeast genetics; gene cloning and deletion; DNA-cellulose binding

timeline.finding: Arabidopsis CDC5 complements the yeast mutant and recombinant AtCDC5 shows sequence-specific binding to CTCAGCG, a sequence contained on the opposite strand of the CIS-BP GCGCTGAGC model.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; yeast complementation; recombinant-protein DNA-binding assays

timeline.finding: Human Cdc5 is reported to bind a 12-bp sequence with high affinity through its N terminus and to activate transcription from it, after earlier attempts by others had failed to find any preferred site for Cdc5-family proteins.
timeline.methods: DNA-binding assays; yeast one-hybrid selection of genomic fragments; reporter assays
timeline.open: Whether the site is used in human cells was not shown.

timeline.finding: CDC5L is found to be part of a multiprotein complex that joins the spliceosome in an ATP-dependent step and is required for the second catalytic step of pre-mRNA splicing.
timeline.methods: Mass spectrometry; immunodepletion and add-back of nuclear extract; in vitro splicing

timeline.finding: AtCDC5, MOS4 and PRL1 are shown to form a conserved complex (MAC) essential for plant innate immunity; AtCDC5 has DNA-binding activity, suggesting transcriptional control.
timeline.methods: Arabidopsis suppressor genetics; protein interaction; DNA-binding assay

timeline.finding: CIS-BP's inference rule transfers measured motifs between proteins with similar DNA-binding domains; by this rule human CDC5L inherits the motif of Arabidopsis CDC5 (87% DBD identity).
timeline.methods: Similarity-based motif inference across eukaryotic DNA-binding domains
timeline.open: The transfer assumes that DBD identity predicts specificity, untested for this protein.

timeline.finding: Cryo-EM of the human catalytic step I spliceosome places the CDC5L-containing complex within the catalytic machinery.
Genome-wide DNase I footprint clustering yields an archetype labelled CDC5L (GATTTAACATA) that bears no resemblance to the plant-derived model.
timeline.methods: DNase I footprinting across 243 cell types; motif clustering
timeline.open: The archetype is named after a motif cluster, not a demonstrated CDC5L binder.

open: Whether human CDC5L acts as a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor in cells is unresolved: a 12-bp high-affinity site and reporter activation were reported in 2000 after earlier failures to find any preferred site, while its established essential role is as a core spliceosome component.

Which, if either, database model describes human CDC5L is unknown: the CIS-BP GCGCTGAGC model is transferred from Arabidopsis CDC5, whose reported site CTCAGCG it contains on the opposite strand, the Vierstra GATTTAACATA archetype is an unrelated footprint cluster, and the relation of either to the 12-bp site reported for the human protein has not been established.
